en: Oṃ. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Oṃ, salutations to Śiva; oṃ, salutations to Sarasvatī; oṃ, salutations to the Guru. There was a daughter of the gods, Yogamāyā, a lore for the sake of the immortals, who was especially worthy of worship and born of the lineage of Bhṛgu. Her son was born on earth, virtuous in character, renowned by the name Mahādeva. Having encountered wicked protectors of the harmful among the people, he abandoned his innate enmity. From him was born Sumativikasat, known as Devadatta, who was wise, possessed of the arts (*kalā*), honored in the assemblies of kings, and like the first flow of the Gaṅgā for the learned. He was an ocean of the nectar of fame whose waves surged in every direction, and whose ears were filled with [the sound of] water.

Whose eyes are awakened by the warbling of cranes, he drinks [the nectar of knowledge]; his son is Gaṅgādhara, who is self-controlled and noble through the qualities of discernment and profundity. Having obtained him, both Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī have surely attained stability at his pair of feet.

Dāmodara became proficient in all the arts; therefore, he is a devotee of Gaṇanātha. Having attained established fame, devoted to his guru and the gods, honored by the virtuous, and dedicated to righteousness, the wise Dāmodara—having seen many Śiva-āgamas, having observed various Saura-āgamas, and having examined extensively the diverse Devī-śāstras and Mahā-āgamas—desires to compose a compendium. He is himself...

For the benefit of the worlds, that bull among the twice-born, having been clearly impelled by the Moon-crested Lord in a dream, composed a manual of yantras known as the *Cintāmaṇi*, joined with mantras. Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa—which was variegated with various minerals, filled with diverse trees and creepers, adorned with many flowers, crowded with hosts of Apsarases, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and inhabited by devotees of Śiva, gods, Daityas, and Pannagas—[he composed it].

It shone, graced by those who know the truth and are uniquely skilled in the meditation of yoga; it was well-served by sentient weapons that uttered cries of victory; it was adorned by thousands of beings with three eyes, two eyes, one eye, or no eyes at all, and by those with three feet, two feet, or one foot—beings who were exceedingly cruel, terrifying, and formidable; it was surrounded on all sides by the guardians of the world headed by Indra, by asuras headed by Bāṇa, and by sages headed by Durvāsas—in such a manner did it shine.

Lord Śiva himself, the God of gods, consisting of light and nectar, inconceivable and eternally auspicious (Sadāśiva), unmanifest yet possessing a manifest form—wherever that Sadāśiva resides, being praised by Viṣṇu and exceedingly joyful, the Supreme Lord, the cause of creation and destruction, seated at one time in solitude, delighted, satisfied, and serene in soul; on that Cintāmaṇi, the best of wish-fulfilling trees, with beautiful leaves, from the mouth of the illustrious Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) emerged [this work], upon which this pedestal was fashioned here by the scholar Dāmodara.

Thus ends the first section in the great kalpa named *Śrī-Yantracintāmaṇi*, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara which bestows direct spiritual realization, as extracted by the scholar Dāmodara Paṇḍita. The playful grace of the Goddess’s braid—she who is the daughter of the Mountain King—is such that for the Lord whose crest is the moon, the moment he beholds it, his state of omniscience is momentarily suspended. Once, having seen the Lord of the Gods, the Goddess, the Mother of the World, with a pure smile, approached and slowly spoke these words. O Goddess!

O Speech, O Śaṅkara, the compassionate Lord of the gods and the world, O my Lord! The duties of the castes and stages of life, my doubts, curiosities, and volitions, as well as the Purāṇas and other scriptures; the application of mantras and the determination of yantras—these are difficult to obtain. Conduct and renunciation in the world, the practice of yoga, and supreme knowledge are rare; the section on yantras is exceedingly rare. Indeed, even the application of many mantras taught in the Vedas is seen [to be so].

Just as it is seen in various scriptural traditions that there is no doubt regarding the destruction of snakes, so too, O twice-born ones, are those who know mantras seen to share in [the removal of] afflictions. O Lord, even for those defeated by heretics, atheists, and revilers of the Vedas, success that fulfills all desires is achieved instantly with little effort through mantras, recitations, and fire-offerings—just as in disputes, legal proceedings, travel, and the conquest of enemies; indeed, O God, all this is accomplished for the practitioner.

"O Lord of the gods, speak the supreme secret that is to be contemplated. Śrī Mahādeva said: "The Vedic conduct has been proclaimed by me for the high-souled sages; the Śiva-dharma for those liberated ones; and the Vaiṣṇava [dharma] for the Vaiṣṇavas. The Saura and Sāṃkhya have been proclaimed by me for many who desire perfection. The Śākta has been taught in many ways, and the Bhairava in many ways, O beloved. Knowledge regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa has indeed been revealed. Yet the secret has been kept hidden everywhere, O auspicious one; of this there is no doubt."

"O lady of excellent hips, even with meditation—and especially so—a mantra devoid of its secret essence does not attain success, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, show me favor! Tell me an easy means that includes the secret, is easy to understand, and produces immediate realization; one that succeeds in the Kali age without fire-offerings, recitation, preliminary rites, or service. Tell us that method. Śrī Śiva said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one who acts for the benefit of the worlds!"

"O lotus-eyed one, I have not been asked about this supreme truth by anyone. Listen with a one-pointed mind to this secret that grants success in an instant. It is named the *Kalpa-cintāmaṇi*, greater than the greatest secrets, the essence of all scriptures, the supreme essence of mantras, and the great essence of essences from the *Atharvaveda*. O Goddess, in this auspicious *Kalpa* consisting of the *Cintāmaṇi*, there will be various yantras that accomplish all desired rites. This..."

If this *lipasandāya* is written and kept in one's home, and is worshipped daily, hear from me its power: there is no fear of untimely death, nor is there fear of thieves; the influence of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* does not arise at all. Surely the deception of another never succeeds. O fair-faced one, the practitioner must not harbor doubt; through doubt, the rite becomes a malevolent spell (*abhicāra*), of this there is no doubt. A yantra performed with doubt produces the opposite result. *Oṃ Rāmoṃ*.

Having bathed and become pure, one should worship the family deity (*kuladevatā*). One should diligently draw this supreme *yantra* in a secluded place; this procedure is proclaimed for whichever ritual application [is intended]. One should perform worship and enjoyments according to the injunctions for three days. For three nights, one should sleep on the ground, remaining chaste and pure. O lady of pure smiles, within three days a dream arises for the practitioner—whether the mantra is already accomplished (*siddha*), yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), or even well-accomplished (*susiddha*)—the presiding deity of the mantra will certainly speak [of it] in the dream when it occurs. When the dream does not arise...

One should declare that which was previously impossible to accomplish as achievable, having heard from the mouth of the deity the attainment of results according to the prescribed rite in a dream; otherwise, one should declare it exactly as it was heard in the dream. Just as [the procedure] was first prohibited in the dream, so too is another supreme yantra.

Having thus inscribed it, whoever performs [the rite], success is proclaimed for him. Having understood these many yantras taught by me, one should adopt whichever yantra or mantra brings about success for those [practitioners], and one should abandon what is prohibited. This is the established rule.

On this earth in the Kali age, practitioners seeking success—whether they be those who have already achieved it (*siddha*), those yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and so forth—behold the yantras, mantras, and seed-syllables (*bīja*) within the treasury of mantras. Yet, in the Kali age, success never arises for them. Nor is there a practitioner in this world who is merely an ordinary person; nor is there a single zodiac sign (*rāśi*), a single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or a single family deity (*kuladevatā*). O Dear One, the yantra, the seed-syllable, and the mantra become fourfold: *siddha*, *sādhya*, *ari* (enemy), and likewise *susiddha*. The *siddha* is mastered in time; the *sādhya* may or may not be mastered; but the *ari* cuts away one's very root.

*Lamsu* is perfected as the bestower of results at that very moment. Therefore, having known the ten spokes, the time, the dream, the rising of the planets, and the mental disposition of the practitioner, one should perform the rite. This supreme secret has been declared by you, which bestows success upon both mantra and yantra. Having understood this, all practitioners on earth shall always become recipients of every accomplishment. [Thus ends the second chapter of the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. *Mahāmohana*: One God alone is victorious—Śiva, the destroyer of all the wicked. Prā...

He who was worshipped by the lotus-eye of Lakṣmī as the Wheel of Generosity (Dānacakra), who is Viṣṇu, who is the graceful Śiva having half his body bestowed upon the daughter of the Mountain, and who bore the Kālakūṭa poison to establish the end of the worlds—Dāmodara, the son of Gādhi, whose intellect is ever fixed on truth, shall now duly proclaim in this excellent Kalpa the various mantras, great scriptures, yantras, and seed-syllables that subjugate kings, wicked men, women, and people alike, as well as many other methods. Śrī Śi... [text ends]

He said: "O Goddess, listen to this most auspicious great yantra for subjugating kings. Having brought a pure vessel of bell-metal that has been treated with ash and other substances, one should engrave it with sandalwood from the *jātī* tree and with yellow pigment (*rocanā*). One should write the name of the person to be influenced in the center; then, one should surround it with a circle. Above that, one should fashion a sixteen-petaled lotus. The vowels beginning with 'a' should be written on each petal in sequence. Then, one should properly enclose that with a line."

Then one should worship with three handfuls (*bhisti*) of *mallikā*, *jātī* flowers, white lotuses, and other fragrant white blossoms. Having thus worshipped that king of diagrams (*yantrarāja*), known as the "Great Enchanter" (*Mahāmohana*), and having performed this for seven days, one should thereafter encase it in the three metals (*triloha*). Whoever—whether a woman or a man—wears it on the head or at the base of the arm, being endowed with firm resolve, all those [servants] will indeed always remain under his control like mere attendants (*kiṅkara*). Thus ends the first diagram, named "The Great Enchanter," in the third section of the chapter on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Oṃ. Śiva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe this yantra known as the Seed-Enclosure (bījasaṃpuṭa), which is excellent for subduing kings and supreme for bringing people under one's control. Having written four *hrīṃ* syllables in a single row, the wise practitioner should then write the name of the person to be influenced (*sādhya*) enclosed within those *hrīṃ* syllables. One should draw this beautiful yantra using yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron, sandalwood paste, and blood from the ring finger. This yantra should be employed whenever [the enemy] is enraged.

When the Lord of Dhūnār sees [the enemy] bound in fetters and his entire wealth destroyed, then one should personally worship this King of Yantras according to the rules with various flowers, food offerings (naivedya), and various auspicious meats. Having worshipped it according to one’s capacity, and having likewise honored the maidens, the Brāhmaṇas, the Yoginīs, and the virtuous women (suvāsinīs) with firm devotion, one should take that Yantra, fastened in the fist, to the palace of the enemy king. This supreme Yantra for subduing by means of nooses pacifies his anger; O Goddess, grace is attained at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. This is the Yantra for pacifying the anger of the King who is the master of the mind of the Yantra-wielder.

Śrī Śiva said: Henceforth, I shall describe a captivating yantra which a man who desires to make his own master subservient for as long as he lives should employ. One should draw two long horizontal lines from south to north. At the ends, one should form a pericarp (karṇikā) both on the south and the north. The practitioner should write the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the word "Śrī," then the name of the person to be subdued (sādhya), and at the end of that, the syllable "Śrīṃ" and the Praṇava again.

Above this, there should be three petals, and likewise three below; one should inscribe them in sequence upon the petals in the south, north, and east, writing the letters from *kṣa* onwards, each accompanied by the visarga.

Having thus written this yantra, which has the seed-syllable *Śrīṃ* in its corners, on a birch leaf with *rocanā* (yellow pigment), one should place it inside that very casket and then seal it with fire. Once it has been removed and cooled to the temperature of one's own body, a person should drink that yantra-ash. For as long as he lives, he will remain under their control; of this there is no doubt. This third [method] is proclaimed as the supreme means for bringing others under one's own power.

Thus ends the third section, concerning the third method for bringing others under one's own power. The illustrious Śiva said: "If anyone’s purpose has been frustrated by someone else, then, through a great ritual application (*mahābhiyoga*), one should employ some divine method..."

To achieve that delusion, the wise man should prepare a divine diagram. On a birch leaf, he should draw a hexagon with *rocanā* (yellow pigment) and saffron. In each corner, the person should write the syllable *hrīṃ*, and in the center, he should likewise write the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Between the corners, he should write six *hrīṃ*s. He should enclose it on all sides with *hrīṃ*s; he should write four *hrīṃ*s above, below, at the front, and at the end.

Having placed that very [name] within the enclosure, he should worship it with a spirit of devotion. On the second day, having drawn out that well-worshipped king of diagrams, and having tied it to his crest-lock at the time of the divine rite, he should [place] the diagram...

A man who remains silent with effort should go there and take the flower with speed; by the grace of this King of Yantras, nothing whatsoever will be difficult to obtain. He shall surely become a divine pillar and attain the state of being meditated upon in the world.

Thus ends the fourth yantra in the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said: When a king is enraged against someone and desires to have him killed, then, for the purpose of deluding that person and for the suppression of the wicked, one should draw the yantra on birch bark using *rocanā* and saffron. One should write *hrīṃ saḥ*, followed by the name of the target (*sādhya*), and then again *hrīṃ saḥ*. Afterwards, one should properly encircle it with four lines.

The wise practitioner should draw a city-line (ṇagarekhā) and write one triangle above and one below; then he should write the syllable *hrīṃ*, the syllable *saḥ*, the syllable *saḥ*, and the syllable *hrīṃ*. Having thus worshipped these four seeds upon each petal, and having placed them within a casket (*saṃpuṭa*), he should worship according to the prescribed rite. Thereby, the mouths of the wicked are paralyzed and they become submissive at that very moment. This is known as the "King-Subduing" (*rājamohana*) mantra, which removes royal wrath and is supreme for the destruction of the wicked.
This should be practiced for seven days until the task is successfully accomplished. Thus ends the fifth yantra, named "King-Subduing," in the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said:

When the Lord, being enraged, truly desires to inflict a blow, then for the sake of protecting one's own life, one should draw the *Mṛtyuñjaya* yantra. Having brought birch-bark leaves, one should write the yantra for the two [protectors]. Having written "Nāma" (the name) in the center, one should draw four corners with lines; thus, one should draw seven sets of four corners with an iron stylus. Upon that, one should write three petals in the four directions. One should write "I" (for Īśāna) and so forth; on the southern petal, "La-la-li-lī-lu-lū"; on the western petal, "Le-le-lo-p"; on the northern petal, "Lau-laṃ-laḥ. Thus, having placed each single seed-syllable on each of the twelve petals.

A person should draw a trident with four corners and a bindu; when these two yantras have been thus described, one should then form a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure). Placing the yantra on the ground, the practitioner, facing north, should certainly scatter level sand over it. Afterwards, he should go toward that [enemy], and his anger will be pacified. This great *Mṛtyuñjaya* yantra is the supreme protector of life; even if the invincible God of Death himself should become enraged against someone, this king of yantras will still protect them—of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the section on subjugation in the third chapter concerning the wicked.

The sixth yantra, named *Vaśīkaraṇa-mṛtyuñjaya*, is as follows. Śrī Śiva said: For the sake of victory in debate, one should construct a beautiful yantra. Having written the name in the center, one should then surround it with a circle. Next, the person should fashion a four-petaled lotus provided with seed-syllables; on each petal, one should write "Hrīṃ Yaṃ Hrīṃ Yaṃ" using yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*). Having drawn this on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*), one should then immerse it in milk. Then, one may go for the purpose of debate and shall be victorious; of this there is no doubt. This yantra, named *Vivāda-vijaya*, is highly honored by the gods. It should not be given to just anyone if one desires success for oneself.

Thus ends the seventh yantra, named *Vivādavijaya* (Victory in Dispute), within the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). The venerable Śiva said: Even when a loss of wealth occurs due to the decree of fate, and a creditor demands his money from a debtor who has become penniless, and he lacks the power to give him any portion of wealth whatsoever—then, for the purpose of deluding him, there is this great *māyāmaya* (illusory) yantra. It should be drawn with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*) upon a wide birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*) in the form of a hexagon (*ṣaṭkoṇa*). [The sequence follows...]

In the center, one should establish the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya-nāma*). Between the corners, three *klīṃ* syllables should be written on the outside; one *klīṃ* syllable should be written situated above the corner.

Then, one should properly encircle that with an excellent circular diagram (*yantra*). One should surround it like a wheel with twenty-five *hrīṃ* syllables. Again, O Dear One, one should properly encircle it with a circle as before. Then, one should worship this *yantra* according to the rules for seven days; thereafter, O Goddess, the wise practitioner should worship it every day during the great festival.

One should recite the excellent *Devīmāhātmya* as declared in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* for seven days; thereafter, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*). At the conclusion, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should feed three young girls. For each verse, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey and clarified butter into the fire. Having encased [an object] in the three metals (*triloha*) at its base or its neck, by merely wearing that, even a wealthy man comes under one's control. He does not ask for wealth, but rather gives it for the sake of trade. Thus ends the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

The eighth [chapter], concerning the ritual for subjugating creditors; Śrī Śiva said: When wicked royal attendants arrive and constantly, day and night, cause one's affairs to become desolate, then one should prepare the great yantra known as "Deluder of the Wicked. Having first written the syllable *NAMA* in the center, one should then encircle it with a circle.

Next, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the seed-syllables thereon; one should place the letter *SA*, ending with the visarga (*ḥ*), in all the corners, and the *Praṇava* (OM) in the primary direction.
Then, one should encircle it on all four sides in sequence with two lines; this beautiful diagram should be drawn on a birch-bark leaf using the blood of a donkey.

Having worshipped this yantra well, one should cast it into the midst of milk. All wicked ones will perish, and it bestows even a kingdom. One should keep the yantra right there for twenty-one days. Thus ends the ninth yantra, named "Deluding the Wicked," in the section on subjugation. Śrī Mahādeva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain this *yantra* which increases victory in dispute, removes fear in legal proceedings, and brings about the breaking of obstacles; it is highly praised. One should draw the syllable *hrīṃ* and likewise the syllable *smāṃ* in the front row. Below that, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), surrounded by a four-cornered enclosure. One should decorate each corner and likewise the central region. In the south, the seed-syllables of obstruction (*rodha-bīja*); in the southwest (*nairṛta*), likewise the syllable *kṣaṃ*; in the west, the seed-syllables of paralysis (*stambha-bīja*); in the northwest (*vāyavya*), likewise the syllable *kṣaṃ*; and in the north, the syllable *kṣo*.

Having thus placed the seed-syllables of Bhava, Īśāna, and Iṅsa in the eight petals, one should place that very King of Yantras within a casket. Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with eight lamps, the world-protectors (Lokapālas) should be well-worshipped and young maidens fed.

Then, having offered oblations and lamps, they should be worshipped in sequence in the eight directions. It should be worshipped with diligence for as long as the task is not accomplished—namely, victory in worldly affairs and in disputes.

"Victory shall come likewise in royal matters and in family disputes; there is no doubt about this. Through the grace of the King of Yantras, his honor shall rise. Thus ends the tenth yantra, named "Victory in Dispute," in the section on subjugation. Śrī Śiva said: "O fair-faced one, if one wishes to bring [others] under one's own control for as long as one lives, then one should prepare this Gāṇapatya yantra which bestows excellent success. Having obtained a broad birch-bark leaf free from holes, [anoint it] with the blood of an elephant mixed with [the blood of] the ring finger."

Likewise, one should combine *mada* (honey), *yāvaka* (lac), resin, and *rocanā* (yellow pigment). Having thus prepared this quartet, one should draw [the diagram] with a *jātī* wood pen. O fair-faced one, seven instances of the syllable *hrīṃ* are to be inscribed in the first row. In the row below, one should likewise inscribe *kroṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, and *gaṃ*. In the fourth row, there should be a quartet of *hrīṃ* syllables.

Having thus inscribed these twenty-two seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should then properly enclose it with a four-cornered line. The syllables *gaṃ* and *śaṃ* are to be inscribed in the east, west, and north.

Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati, one should place a yantra within its belly. Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should recite this mantra: "O God of gods, Lord of the hosts, saluted by gods and asuras! O Lord, make Devadatta subject to me for as long as I live. Having uttered this mantra and buried [the image] to the depth of a cubit, and having placed the Lord of the hosts there, one should fill it with earth. By the grace of Gaṇanātha, the person shall remain under one's control for as long as one lives.

Thus, in the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the eleventh yantra called *Gāṇapatya*, the eleventh [chapter]. Śrī Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that auspicious method which brings about subjugation. Having written the syllable *Nā* (Na) in the center, the wise man should write the syllable *Ī*. Having encircled it three times upon a wide birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*), he should then draw a four-petalled lotus in the four directions starting from the east. "Oṃ namaḥ" should be written in the west and "oṃ namaḥ" in the east.

Then, one should write "Oṃ Ajite Oṃ Ajite" on the right and the left; this is the enchanting King of Yantras named *Janavaśyakara* (the subduer of people). A man devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should worship it daily for three days. On the fourth day, being firm in his vows, he should feed a single Brāhmaṇa. Having encased it with the three metals, he should wear it upon his upper arm, or especially on a cord of silk, whether made of gold or silver. This most excellent yantra should be worn at the base of the arm or on the throat for the sake of all.

And this procedure for the yantras has been proclaimed: by wearing this yantra, O Goddess, one becomes fortunate, handsome, and beloved by one's own kin; of this there is no doubt. It should be drawn with camphor, saffron, and likewise with *gorocana*. Thus ends the twelfth yantra, named "The Subjugation of People," in the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, to the most auspicious great yantra that brings the world under control. [It is drawn] with camphor, musk, sandalwood, and likewise with *gorocana*.

One should inscribe it upon birch bark, especially using *jātī* wood. First, one should write the five seed-syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) in the first row: *praṇava*, *va*, *ja*, *hrīṃ*, and *ḍa*. Then, in the second row, one should inscribe *daṇḍa*, *hrīṃ*, *praṇava*, and likewise *ka*; after that, the syllable *va*, which is the name of the world (*jagannāma*); and immediately following that, one should certainly write the fourth syllable, *ṭha*, and then the syllable *dī*.

Then, at the end, having thus inscribed the five seed-syllables (*bījapañcaka*), one should establish a four-cornered figure. This great work, which brings the world under control, should be fashioned with two lines and encased in three metals; one should wear it upon the upper arm. The world comes under his control as long as this yantra remains [with him]. Having first worshipped the yantra daily during the rites of deity worship and so forth—thus ends the thirteenth yantra, named "Bringing the World Under Control," in the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śiva said: When one’s own servant, being angry, reveals the entire right path, then...

For the purpose of deluding others and for the accomplishment of one's own aims, it is not possible to repel [this power] even by the force of place and time. A wise person should construct a yantra called *piśācikā*. Having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a circle.

With diligence, one should draw a beautiful four-petaled lotus provided with seed-syllables; one should inscribe the syllable *hrīṃ* in the middle of each of the four petals in the four directions. A man should write this on birch bark with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) using a stylus. Then, he should place it within the center of those petals as spoken by Rudra. Thus ends the *Piśācikā* named "Subduing Servants" in the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

The Fourteenth Yantra, named *Khyam*. Śrī Śiva said: When a master of cruel nature is served by people, even though he is being served intensely, he never gives anything at all. A king who is constantly surrounded by wicked men and is of evil conduct—whether he be high-born or low-born, or even a barbarian (*mleccha*)—if one performs the *Kālānala* yantra, it will bring him under one's control and grant success. The letters of the name of the person to be influenced (*sādhya*) should be written so as to enter within the syllable *hrīṃ*. As many letters as there are in the name, that many instances of *vahnīṃ* (the seed-syllable of fire) and likewise the letter *ī* should be written at the end. This should be inscribed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*). [It should be] repeated three times...

One should fashion a fruit-shaped object with four corners and a long base, and make an image of *rājikā* (black mustard) for its foot. One should place the dust from that [foot] inside it, and within that, insert the great *Kālānala* yantra. Having worshipped that image, one should bury it at the side of the dust heap. One should worship it with diligence on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) at the dead of night. By merely performing this, [the target] will certainly become submissive, [mixed] with the blood of a cat.

Likewise, an offering of rice-balls (*pūpa*) and a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) should always be presented for the pleasure of the divine ones. One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the mantra: *oṃ mahākāli svāhā*. That same rice, mixed with clarified butter and well-worshipped with red flowers, [is offered] upon the diagram named Kālānala, which is worshipped even by the gods. Thus ends the fifteenth diagram, named Kālānala, concerning the fierce subjugation within the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said: Regarding commerce...

When one has gone to the place of weighing and sees that not even one among them harbors a wicked intent on the path, then the master should fashion this yantra. A person should write the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center, with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) inside it; above it, in the four directions, he should write the mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*. In the center, he should write "attract" (*ākarṣaya*), and then sequentially in the four directions. Afterwards, he should enclose that yantra within a quadrangle of two lines, and at each corner, he should fashion two tridents. Having thus prepared this excellent yantra and worshipped it with diligence, [he should smear it] with his own blood.

Having written [the mantra] mixed with *rocanā* on a birch leaf and fashioned it into a sword-shaped amulet, one should place it in secret; at that very moment, even a most cruel man becomes submissive. Thus ends the sixteenth yantra, named "The Piśāca of Remnants," for subduing the wicked, within the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said: When a powerful enemy seeks to carry out his designs...

If one desires that [the target] act in accordance with one's will, one should prepare a thorny yantra. One should write the name of the person to be influenced in the center and surround it with a circle. Then, having written the syllable *ī*, the syllable *bhyo*, and [the syllable *pha*] ending in a visarga in each of the four directions, one should again surround them with a circle. This should be drawn with cremation ashes upon two *arka* leaves. Having joined them together as a casket, one should then enclose it with thorns. Having worshipped it at night in a cremation ground, one should bury the yantra and fill it over.

Then, having offered the oblation (*balipradāna*), a man who acts with diligence on that day becomes an enemy at that very moment; yet he becomes well-disposed toward him, without a doubt. This great machine (*yantra*) called "The Thorn" (*kaṇṭaka*) is supreme for deluding the wicked. One should give it according to one's capacity, saying: "May Kālarātri be pleased. Thus ends the seventeenth machine, titled "Making an Enemy Well-Disposed," within the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said: Or [one may act] toward a friend...

If either an enemy faction or a kinsman becomes angry, then a wise person should construct a yantra for the purpose of pacifying that anger. Having written the letter *nā* in the center, one should then encircle it; having likewise encircled it in the four directions—above, below, to the north, and to the south—one should write it excluding the central dot (*bindu*). One should write the syllable *hūṃ* within the interior, in the middle of the dot, above, below, to the south, and to the north, including the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) as before.

Endowed with the syllable *hūṃ* at the end, one should propitiate [the deity] in the lower row. Having inscribed this yantra on a wide palm leaf, one should sew it with thorns. On a Monday, having placed this yantra inside a ball made of the clay from a potter’s kiln, one should perform worship with diligence; thereby, the anger of Jamadagni—the supreme mantra that instantly removes wrath—is pacified. One should be free from anger and truthful in speech.

"Jamadagni of firm vows, the progenitor of Rāma, you who are the very embodiment of truth—salutations to you! Having recited this mantra at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform it daily for seven days; this is the supreme method for removing anger. On the seventh day, a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas should be fed; otherwise, raw food should be given to satisfy his hunger. Thus, anger departs from the heart and one becomes serene in an instant.

Thus ends the eighteenth yantra, named "The Pacification of Anger," belonging to Jamadagni, within the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said: "O Goddess, hereafter I shall speak of those [yantras] which destroy misfortune."

Having drawn in a single row the diagrams that increase the good fortune and enchant the lovers of women, O auspicious one, having written three *hrīṃ* syllables, one should write beneath them the name of Vairamaṇa. Then, in the third row, one should again write three *hrīṃ* syllables. Thereafter, one should properly enclose it with a four-cornered line. Then, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus, one should arrange the seed-syllables (*bīja*).

The wise practitioner should place a *hrīṃ* syllable on each petal and at each corner. Having mixed together yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron, musk, and sandalwood, one should draw the diagram upon a wide birch-bark leaf. [Note: The final word "trayo" appears to be a scribal error for "traye" (locative singular), referring to the birch-bark.]

On the tenth day of the dark fortnight, the practitioner, facing north, should worship that yantra every night, O fair-faced one, with various kinds of offerings, flowers, garments, ornaments, and decorations. Having performed this for seven days, at its conclusion, for your satisfaction, he should feed seven women endowed with good fortune, saying: "O beloved of Śaṅkara, O Lalitā, may you be pleased! Grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me good fortune!"

"O Himeṃbike, O Bhagavatī, grant me fortune, my desired wish, and a long life. Having recited this mantra, one should then offer the *arghya* (water of respect). Then, having encased that yantra with metal, one should wear it around one's neck; thus, one shall become fortunate, endowed with beauty, and exceedingly beloved. This great yantra named Lalitā brings about good fortune for women. Thus ends the nineteenth yantra, titled "The Bringer of Good Fortune for Women," belonging to the deity Lalitā, within the section on subjugation (*vaśyādhikāra*). Śrī Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the yantra that propitiates one’s husband. Having drawn the auspicious name of the beloved, enclosed within the syllable *śāṃ*, [one should worship it].

Above and below, one should draw two auspicious lines in the form of the letter *śāṃ*; then, one should properly encircle that with a single circular line. Above that, one should write eight petals together with the syllable *hrīṃ*. A person should write this on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) using yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*). One should worship it daily for three days at night, O beloved, as before. Then, on the fourth day, one should worship the three beautiful goddesses during the night, saying: "O Goddess, Beloved of Anaṅga, may you be pleased with me."

"O beloved of Smara, perform this great subjugation which is dear to you! Having recited this mantra and worshipped those women, one should fashion that yantra from metal and wear it around the neck; by the grace of this king of yantras, the husband shall become a slave. Incomparable good fortune arises for her—of this there is no doubt. This yantra, which increases good fortune, must not be given to anyone and everyone. Thus ends the twentieth yantra, named "The Bestower of Good Fortune," within the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Mahādeva said: "I shall proclaim the subjugation of women; listen, O Goddess, to this most auspicious [method]. With *rocanā* (cow bezoar) and saffron..."

Having written the yantra on birch bark with sandalwood paste and musk using a stylus made of jasmine wood, one should enclose it within a four-cornered figure. The wise practitioner should carefully write the five seed-syllables above and below: *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, then the name, then again *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*. Having thus formed the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭita*), one should place the seed-syllables in the corners: *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ* and likewise *kṣāṃ aiṃ* at the end. Thus, the syllables *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ* are to be arranged in the corners in that very same manner.

A lotus shape should be drawn, with seeds arranged around it; having thus fashioned a beautiful four-petaled lotus provided with seed-syllables, one should fashion an image of Rājikā from the wood of Madana. Having thoroughly worshipped that [image] in the heart, one should then install the yantra. With various enjoyments, perfumes, incenses, lamps, and auspicious fruits, one should worship it daily at the end of each day, both night and day, O auspicious lady. When this is done, that woman shall become a servant.

This supreme machine known as Śrī Kāmarāja, which brings women under one's control, is not produced [by mere words]. Here, Madana should be worshipped by men using *rājikā* (black mustard) images. "Kāma, Anaṅga, Pañcaśara, Kandarpa, Mīnaketana, the son of Śrī Viṣṇu—O Lord, be gracious unto me! This shall be the mantra for worship, O lotus-eyed one. Thus it must be performed daily until she comes under subjection; no doubt should be entertained here—so said Janārdana. Thus ends the twenty-first machine, named Kāmarāja, concerning the subjugation of women within the section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain...

This machine for crushing pride, which crushes the pride of those who imagine themselves superior, is very difficult to find in the world; it is renowned as the *Madanamardana* (the Destroyer of Lust). On a leaf of birch-bark (*bhūrjapatra*) smeared with the blood of a horse and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), one should write the syllable *Oṃ* (*praṇava*), then *Hrīṃ*, and then the letters of the name of the person to be subjugated (*sādhya*) separately.

All the letters of the name should be enclosed by the syllable *Hrīṃ*. The syllable *Oṃ* should be written at the beginning and at the end by one of good intellect, all in a single line. Then, one should properly enclose that with four lines, drawing them above and below as before.

One should fashion a seed-capsule (bījasaṃpuṭa) with the shape of a drum (mardala) at its center and the form of a cornered vessel at its edges. Having well-drawn this yantra, one should fashion an auspicious image of Madana out of the wood of Madana and place it within the heart; one should make the heart hollow so that the yantra remains therein. Having wrapped it, one should certainly cast the yantra clearly upon his chest and worship it daily with red sandalwood and garlands. Thus [ends] the Śrī-vaśīkara...

In the section on the subjugation of women, here is the twenty-second yantra, named *Madanamardana* (the Crusher of Passion). Śrī Mahādeva said: Hereafter I shall describe the method for subjugating royal women, by whose mere glance they fall suddenly as if struck by the arrows of Kāma, overwhelmed with constant intoxication. A man should write this yantra upon birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) using yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and camphor (*karpūra*), according to the prescribed method for jasmine wood (*jātīkāṣṭha*).

Then, in the center of that hexagon, one should inscribe the syllable *Kroṃ*, established by its name, upon all the corners on every side. In the space between the eastern corner and the next, the syllable *Hrīṃ* is situated in the east. Afterwards, one should encircle all of that with an auspicious circular line. To the south, one should make a three-petaled lotus; likewise, the syllable *Hrīṃ* should be placed in each petal. One should inscribe the syllable *Hrīṃ* in the middle of each petal in due order. Having thus inscribed it—

One should worship the yantra with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and food offerings, while wearing white garments oneself. Standing before the yantra at night, one should meditate upon that woman. Having performed this for seven days, at its conclusion, three Brahmins should be fed various kinds of foods with the prayer, "May Kāmākhya be pleased. According to one's means, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and feed the female practitioner. Then, having encased [the yantra] in the three metals...

If one wears it on the root of the arm, the king’s beloved wife, afflicted by the arrows of Kāmadeva, will constantly seek him out herself; what need is there to speak of other women? Thus ends the twenty-third yantra, named *Kāma*, which subdues the wives of kings, in the third section on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-vaśīkaraṇādhikāra*. The venerable Mahādeva said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim a single seed-mantra (*bīja*) of great fruit, which whoever wears constantly—

He shall become most beloved by women; if a woman wears [this] with devotion, she shall become possessed of good fortune. This seed-syllable is the producer of good fortune for men in particular; therefore, that seed-syllable must be kept secret and should not be given to just anyone. In the *Uḍīśa*: To subjugate a woman, one should collect white *guñjā* under the Puṣya asterism and, on a Sunday, apply a *tilaka* (forehead mark) together with *gorocanā* and saffron. She will then become overwhelmed and infatuated by the arrows of Kāma. One should apply the *tilaka* consecrated with this mantra: *Oṃ aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hruṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the *Kāmabāṇa-tilaka*.

One should write [the mantra] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (nīra), joining the six syllables in this sequence: the letter *sa*, the letter *ha*, the letter *va*, likewise the letter *la*, the letter *ci*, and ending with the letter *ī*. It is conjoined with the vowel *ī* and adorned above with the *bindu*. Having performed worship for three days, one should then enclose it in gold; a man should wear this king of seed-syllables (*bījarāja*) at the base of his arm, and likewise a woman on her heart. [By doing so,] misfortune will clearly vanish.

"The destroyer of ignorance and the generator of great good fortune, established by Śrī Śiva. Thus ends the twenty-fourth yantra, named "The Generator of Good Fortune," in the third section of the chapter on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Śrī Mahādeva said: "Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra that bestows good fortune. This yantra known as 'Kamala' is specifically intended for women. By wearing it, O Goddess, even a barren woman becomes pregnant. For that woman who has lost her children, this yantra is most excellent. [It should be] worn..."

O Goddess, there is no doubt that a man whose son is living shall never be separated from him. A man should write [this mantra] on a birch leaf using *rocana* and saffron. First, he should write the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and immediately after that, the syllable *hrīṃ*. Then, the name of the beloved one should be established, ending with *hrīṃ*.

He should write the syllable *kroṃ* once above and once below. Then, he should encircle all of that again with a circular line. Above that, he should place eight petals joined with seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*), and he should place the syllable *hraṃ* in the middle of the petals in the four directions. Oṃ.

One should likewise write the syllable *kāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *juṃ*, and again *hrīṃ*; thus these four seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be written. A leaf should be drawn in each corner, and the practitioner [should place the name] in the central region. Having thus well-drawn this yantra, one should worship it for three days. One should feed a single couple with the thought, "May the Lord of the World be pleased. Afterwards, having wound it with thread—and especially with gold—one should fashion it into a circle like a jewel and wear it in the middle of a necklace. O Goddess, through wearing it, good fortune is produced.

"By this great *matula* [yantra], one whose sons are living shall surely become barren, and even a barren woman shall perish. This great *yantra* named *Kamala* was created by Brahmā in ancient times; it must not be given to just anyone, O fair-faced one, by the practitioner (*sādhaka*). Thus ends the twenty-fifth *yantra*, named *Kamala*, in the third section extracted by Paṇḍita Dāmodara, within the chapter on subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara from the *Yantracintāmaṇi*, the Great Kalpa that bestows manifest success. Śrī Śiva said:

[Thus ends the section on subjugation. [Now begins the section on attraction. Victorious is the Great Lord Maheśa, whose immeasurable splendor is the very embodiment of command; who illuminates the entire world with divine months and the radiance of his pure rays; whose moon-crested head throbs with light; whose beautiful smile flashes amidst the great, venomous serpents; and who is eternally possessed of infinite power. Now this fourth pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) is commenced within the *Cintāmaṇi*, the best of manuals—the clear exposition of the mechanical diagrams for attraction.

In the introductory section (*pīṭhikā*), one should write the name on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*) and, in its center, draw the four-syllabled mantra that attracts with *gorocanā*, ending with the seed-syllable *sa* joined with the *visarga*.

Above that, one should draw the yantra, having placed the syllable *īṃ* in the middle; from there, one should write the syllables *sa* joined with the *visarga*, as well as *kroṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *kroṃ*, in a row according to the great sequence of the letters. Thus, it is arranged in two rows.

Having first written [the syllable] *ca*, one should then write the line in the middle of the name; having likewise written *hrīṃ kroṃ* and then *hrīṃ* and *kroṃ*, one should write them in the lower portion of the name. Having written *hrīṃ kroṃ* and then *hrīṃ* in that line, one should then write the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) below it—the letters *da* and *ra*. Afterward, one should encircle it three times with a surrounding circle. Then, having worshipped the yantra according to the rules and subsequently encircled it with a very white thread, [one should perform] the rubbing away (*udvartana*) with one's own...

Having certainly fashioned an image from the bodily excretions of the person, and having placed this king of yantras within its heart, one should subsequently heat it for three days with a fire of *khadira* wood at the three junctions of the day while reciting the excellent mantras.

Now, the mantra for heating is: *devadattaṃ vegena ākarṣaya maṇibhadra svāhā*. When this is done, Maṇibhadra will surely draw the person toward him even if they are in another land; by means of this yantra, he shall bring even those situated at an extreme distance under his control in due course.

"Indeed, Māṇibhadra, when thus well-worshipped during the descent [of the deity], immediately attracts even those who are pure in fame. Thus ends the first yantra, named the Attraction of Māṇibhadra, in the fourth section of the Chapter on Attraction.

The illustrious Mahādeva said: "Hereafter I shall describe the yantra for the vision of Mitra. Having written the name in the center with red sandalwood mixed with the blood of the ring finger upon a birch bark leaf, one should then encircle it with a circle and [draw] a four-petaled lotus."

One should then fashion a captivating *hūṃ* syllable joined with the seed-syllable and write it individually and in sequence in the center of each petal. Having thus thoroughly worshipped this yantra with charming offerings of food and flowers, one should place it within clarified butter; indeed, attraction will occur within three days. This yantra is to be kept strictly secret and must be guarded with great effort; it should not be given to just anyone if one desires success for oneself. Thus ends the second [chapter], named "The Meeting with a Friend," in the fourth section of the *Ākarṣaṇādhikāra*.

Then Śrī Mahādeva said: "Now, therefore, I shall fully describe this great *yantra* that fulfills all desires. A person should write it on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) mixed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*nīra*). Having first written the auspicious syllable *Hrīṃ* in the center, one should then draw a beautiful six-cornered hexagon containing the name [of the practitioner]. One should inscribe the syllable *Sauṃ* in each corner, adorned with a dot (*bindu*) in the center. After worshipping this *yantra* well, one should place it in the midst of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and worship it every day."

If one should pray daily again to Tripurā: "By your great speed, attract to me my beloved Devadatta!"—saying "Oṃ Aiṃ! O Tripurā, O Mistress of Gods, I shall give what has been requested to you"—one should worship the Tripurā Yantra with this mantra while praying. When this is done, on the seventh day, O auspicious one, attraction indeed occurs. Thus ends the third [section], the Tripurā Attraction Yantra, in the chapter on Attraction. Śrī Mahādeva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious attraction of a woman, which is the secret of all Yantras and bestows success instantly. This King of Yantras should not be given to just anyone. It is most...

One should draw the syllable *ṣka* with the blood of one's own ring finger on the left palm; likewise, a man should write the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), as well as *klīṃ klīṃ*, in a single line. One should then write the three instances of *svāhā* in sequence below that. Below that again, O observer of good vows, one should write the name of the beloved woman. Afterwards, O Dear One, one should encircle the triangle above the seed-syllables (*bījas*). Having done this and worshipped it there with auspicious flowers, that woman will arrive within just one watch (three hours) of the night; of this there is no doubt. This is the Yantra known as Śrī Kāmarāja, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. Thus ends the fourth Yantra, called the Śrī Lalanākṛṣṭi Kāmarāja.

The illustrious Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *yantra* known as the Vaidevamātrika, which captivates both men and women; listen, O Goddess, to its great fruit. This supreme *yantra* should be diligently inscribed by oneself alone on a birch leaf using lac juice, turmeric, and madder. Having first drawn a triangle in the center, one should then encircle it; thereafter, O Beloved, one should carefully encircle that with a circle. Above that, the sixteen vowels and the consonants beginning with 'ka' should be written, and then one should encircle all of that with a line numbering twenty (two times ten). Then, from the dust of its own feet, one should fashion a *śālabhañjikā* (wooden doll); of that—

Having drawn and worshipped the King of Yantras (Yaṃtrarāja) upon a piece of cloth, when this is done, she will be attracted and arrive; of this there is no doubt. What more need be said here? One should bring her along with her child. This King of Yantras, known as Devamātṛka, is to be kept strictly secret.

Thus ends the fifth yantra, known as Devamātṛka, for the attraction of proud women, within the section on Attraction (Ākarṣaṇādhikāra) in the *Cintāmaṇikalpavara*. The section on Attraction is complete. This is the excellent and wonderful yantra.

When that [text] had issued from the mouth of the illustrious Śrīcaṇḍacūḍa, the eminent Brāhmaṇa Dāmodara composed this fourth pedestal (pīṭhikā). The third great section, named Ākarṣaṇa, which possesses great power, is now complete. Five extremely powerful yantras have been proclaimed as being of a secret nature. Some always call her Nārāyaṇī, while others declare her to be Viśvamātṛ; I bow to that Goddess of the Universe, the bestower of fearlessness, who is praised by hosts of Gandharvas, Siddhas, gods, and Yakṣas, and who consists of the three qualities (guṇas). Now follows the consideration of the great section named Saṃstambhana.

"Listen now, O Goddess, to the yantras and seed-syllables (*bījas*) on this pedestal, which are suppressive (*stambhana*) and grant success in an instant. The venerable Śiva said: "Listen, O Goddess, to the great yantra that paralyzes all enemies. In disputes and legal proceedings, the paralysis of the mouth shall certainly occur. When, O Goddess, a quarrel arises by the force of time, then one should fashion the great yantra that supremely pierces the tongue.

It should be well-drawn by the wise upon a *bhūrja* leaf with yellow pigment (*rocanā*). One should form eight hexagons with two lines each; in the center of each square, one should write a single seed-syllable."

The letter *ha*, the letter *ma*, and the letter *la* immediately following; then the letter *va*, the letter *ṛ*, and ending with the letter *ya* firmly established; joined with the vowel *ū*, adorned with the letter *ra* at its head, and joined with the half-measure of the *bindu*—this group of six letters within the square [is formed]. Joined with two vowels and adorned above with the *bindu*, thus the seed-syllable (*bīja*) arises, which is supreme for paralyzing the mouth. Each of these supreme seed-syllables should be written individually in each square. Thus the seed-syllables are to be written with two lines, having placed them above the seed-syllables in the corner regions of the four directions.

The outer lines should be drawn above and below, with tridents (triśūla) at their tops; on every side, one should draw tridents at the end of each line in sequence. One must certainly write the six seed-syllables (bīja) beginning with *Ṭhaṃ* both above and below, as many as there are, likewise in the southern direction and similarly in the north. After writing the names of Śrī and Sūrya, one should worship the yantra according to rule with great effort. Then, with a steady mind, one should recite the mantra mentally at the three junctions of the day for three days with diligence. Now, the mantra is: *Hrllūlastambhaya stambhaya*.

"Amukasya amukhaṃ staṃbhaya staṃbhaya svāhā. This should be recited one hundred and eight times. One should worship this excellent yantra at the three junctions of the day with beautiful yellow flowers as bright as gold. When done in this manner, this supreme yantra will certainly paralyze the movement and the mind of the enemy. The formidable enemy becomes utterly bewildered and speechless, like one seized by a malevolent planet. Thus ends the first yantra for the paralysis of an enemy's mouth.

Śrī Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme *staṃbhana* (paralyzing rite). Having beautifully inscribed it upon a stone slab with yellow substances—namely, *rocanā*, *haritāla*, turmeric (*haridrā*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) mixed with saffron (*kuṅkuma*)—which are known as the yellow substances; a person should write the seed-syllables of *moha* in a single row. Below that, one should write the name established at the end of the word *moha*. Then, one should properly enclose it within a four-cornered line, with a trident in each corner and likewise in the center of each [section]; thus there are eight tridents.

O beloved, having prepared the yantra, worship it with yellow flowers—such as karṇikāra, kurṇṭha, campaka, golden ketakī, dhattūra, yellow-colored nāgakesara, and so forth; O fair-faced one, these flowers should be taken according to their availability, and other yellow-colored flowers are never to be used. With these flowers, the king of yantras becomes most beautiful; worship it thus with incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of edibles. Having worshipped in this manner...

Then, one should place the yantra in the middle of the ground and fill it with earth, carefully on top of the yantra in that spot; this will certainly arrest movement—of this there is no doubt. O beloved, even if a vessel is placed upon it, it will never move. Thus ends the second yantra, named "Arresting Travel," in the section on Stambhana. Śrī Mahādeva said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme "Arresting of Speech" (vāṇī-stambhana). This yantra, known on earth as the "Arrestor of the Opponent's Mouth," should be drawn with yellow substances inside a stone casket.

Having drawn a triangle in the center, one should then encircle it; thereafter, one should properly enclose that again with a circular line. Above that, one should fashion eight petals. In the middle of each petal, the letter *la* adorned with a bindu should be inscribed. Thus, having drawn the eight-petaled [lotus], one should worship it with auspicious flowers—specifically yellow blossoms—as well as with lamps and excellent food offerings (*naivedya*). One should feed a single Brāhmaṇa with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and jaggery. Then, O Dear One, one should bury it in the ground or install it as before during a dispute.

In the discussion of debate and in the exposition of the scriptures, this [mantra] causes the mouth of the opponent to become paralyzed; of this there is no doubt. O Great Goddess, this yantra has been told to you as something to be well-guarded in secret.
Thus, in the third chapter of the fifth section, the third yantra, named "The Paralysis of the Opponent’s Mouth," has reached its conclusion. Śrī Mahādeva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sealing of the enemy's mouth (*śatruvaktramudraṇa*). O lady of excellent vows, when a dispute arises with an enemy, one should then construct this easily accessible yantra which grants success in an instant. O Beloved, it should be swiftly drawn with chalk upon one’s own wall. Having first written the name of the enemy in the center according to the prescribed rite, one should then draw eight lines above it, proceeding from the eight directions. At the end of each line in the eight directions, O Goddess, one should draw tridents. There, having worshipped well with white flowers and auspicious fruits, as well as other [offerings]...

With white perfumes and beautiful white garments, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa while saying, "May Śrī Śiva be pleased. In debates and in the assembly of scholars, this [rite] causes the mouth of the opponent to become paralyzed. Thus ends the fourth yantra, named "Paralyzing the Mouth of the Opponent," in the section on Paralysis within the fifth chapter of the *Śrī-pañcamapīṭhikā*. Śrī Mahādeva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the enchanting paralysis of fire (*vahnistambha*). One should perform this most beautiful king of yantras at an auspicious time, having drawn it upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf using yellow pigments.

One should write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended in the center, enclosed within *kroṃ mlāṃ kroṃ*. One should then write the beautiful syllable *kroṃ* above and below it. Then, O Goddess, one should encircle that with a four-cornered line.

Above that, one should fashion another four-cornered figure with two lines. Between the corners, one should inscribe the seed-syllables of the letter *la*. At the end of each corner, O Dear One, a trident should be drawn separately on all sides. Having thus drawn the eight tridents, one should then worship them. After worshipping, the Brāhmaṇa should feed [the deity] and cast the yantra upon the ground. Having placed the yantra in the middle of a flowing stream or on a path, [one should proceed].

As long as water is poured over it, for that long a great pillar of fire arises; of this there is no doubt. This machine, named the Divine Support (*divyasaṃstambhana*), is highly honored by the gods. It must not be given to just anyone if one desires success for oneself. Thus ends the fifth machine, called the Divine Fire-Support, in the glorious fifth section. The illustrious Mahādeva said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the machine for the warding off of fire. In whichever house that machine exists, there is never any fear of fire. In whosever house this enchanting king of machines always resides, even in dreams he has no fear of fire.

O Beloved, the taking up of fire should never be performed by force; likewise, when the machine or the medicine is present, it is superior in power. Just as a snake, when touched by the foot, bites without a doubt, so too, O Lord of Gods, even a pillar [of paralysis] causes untimely death through the force of people, O Goddess, just as a physician’s elixir [acts]. In the same way, O Lord of Gods, the machine also paralyzes; there is no doubt in this matter. Śrī...

Having written one's own name according to the prescribed rite in the center of a large, beautiful birch leaf using a mixture of sugar, *rocanā*, *niśā* (turmeric), and excellent saffron, one should encircle it with a circular line and likewise draw four petals around it with lines. Then, having worshipped this yantra—which is the God of gods—daily in the middle of the house, or in milk, or otherwise, with the letter *va* joined with the nasal bindu (*vṃ*) in the east, west, north, and south, no fear shall ever arise for him from fire. Furthermore, for the satisfaction of the King of Yantras, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the sixth yantra, named "The Stilling of Fire," within the section on "Stilling" in the fifth book. Śrī Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme method for stilling a lover, O fair-faced one, so that when a man becomes angry even though he has been restrained, one may employ this extensive yantra for the purpose of stilling his anger. It should be drawn with yellow substances upon a wooden board made of wood.

The yantra may be made of crystal, or it may be drawn on a wooden board made of crystal. In the center, within the letter *la*, the name of the person to be paralyzed (*sādhya*) should be established. Then, one should properly encircle it with four lines forming a square. Above that, the wise practitioner should draw a second square. In each corner, he should form the shape of the letter *la*, and in the middle space, separately, he should write the letter *la* joined with a bindu (anusvāra), O Dear One.

Having thus drawn this excellent yantra and worshipped it according to the rules, one should then place the board face down in the middle of the house; by that means, O Goddess, paralysis shall occur—of this there is no doubt.

"Nevertheless, even as he goes, having gone, he returns. Thus ends the sixth yantra, named "The Stopping of the Departure of a Beloved," in the section on Stambhana within the illustrious fifth Pīṭhikā. Śrī Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for paralyzing the speech of enemies. One should well-inscribe it with chalk inside a stone casket, with the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center and the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) established therein.
Then, one should properly encircle it with three lines forming a square. Above that, having drawn another supreme yantra in a square, one should place four tridents at each of the four corners.

One should draw the yantra and worship it according to the rules with auspicious flowers; having written it within a casket, one should place that auspicious yantra therein. At that very moment, the enemy’s mouth will be paralyzed, of this there is no doubt. One should feed a single Brāhmaṇa, saying, "May Śiva be pleased with me. Thus ends the seventh yantra, named "Paralyzing the Enemy's Mouth," in the section on Paralysis.

Śrī Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra for sealing the mouths of slanderers. O God, whenever someone becomes a slanderer toward one's own family, then [one should employ] this yantra...

O fair-faced one, I shall describe the auspicious seal that paralyzes the speech, movement, and intellect of an enemy. One should write a beautiful diagram on a leaf of *bhūrja* with *rocanā* (cow bezoar).

One should enclose the syllable arising from the name with the syllable *Kroṃ*. Then, the second syllable should likewise be enclosed with the syllable *Hrīṃ*. This process of enclosing should be done for as many syllables as there are in the name. Then, one should properly surround it with four lines forming a square. In each corner, one should fashion a petal joined with a long seed-syllable (*dīrghabīja*), namely the letter *Ya*, the letter *Ma*, and the letter *Ra*, and likewise [the letter *La*].

One should write the letter *ca*, then *va*, then *ci*, and immediately after that *ya*; having thus joined these six letters in sequence, one should write them in the middle of the petals, well-conjoined with the vowel *u*, adorned at the head with the letter *ra*, and endowed with the nasal bindu (*m*). Having thus drawn the four-petaled [lotus], which is indeed the seed-syllable worshipped by the gods, one should write *kroṃ* and *kṣa* in the intermediate spaces between the petals and in the four directions. Having thus drawn the yantra, one should worship it with red sandalwood, red flowers, and red garments, O beautiful one; and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) made of copper should be given according to one's capacity.

One should draw [the diagram] on a cloth from a cemetery using a pen made of a crow’s feather and with the blood of a sheep. Having seen charcoal produced from a cremation ground, one should write the name of the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) and then surround it with a triangle. One should then draw two lines each above and below; subsequently, during the nights of the *bhūta* days (the eighth and fourteenth), one should properly enclose that with a square line. Tridents should be drawn in every corner facing the four directions, situated upon four petals directed toward the four quarters. Having thus drawn the yantra, one should worship it according to the rules, then bury it seven finger-breadths deep and fill the middle of the ground over it, whether while staying or during a journey.

O beloved, when this machine is cast upon the path, a great mutual hatred arises among kinsmen. Or, if one draws it on the leaf of a tree, that person too becomes a vessel for misfortune; of this there is no doubt, by the power of the King of Machines. Thus ends the third machine, named "Causing Hatred Among Kinsmen," in the section on incantations for creating enmity. Śrī Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the method for causing hatred between master and servant.

On a cloth from a cremation ground, using a pen made of a crow’s feather mixed with red and hateful substances, one should draw [the diagram] at midnight on the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī). One should write the name of the target (sādhya) in the center and then encircle it with a circle. Ta...

Furthermore, one should write three *rakāra*s (ra) above and below it; in the horizontal section, the three-fold worship (*tripūjaka*) should be written enclosed by two *yakāra*s; and the *makāra* and *yakāra* ending with the *visarga* are established [therein]. Having thus inscribed the yantra, one should encircle it again with a circle. When this yantra is well-inscribed and buried in their path, constant and great hatred arises between the master and the servant as long as the yantra remains in the earth.

Thinking that "hatred proceeds excessively," there may arise intense enmity between master and servant. Thus ends the fourth yantra, named "Causing Enmity Between Master and Servant," in the section on instilling hatred.

Śrī Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe that supreme yantra which causes hatred in the world, which is terrifying by name, and which increases misfortune. With the blood of a crow or an owl, or again with human blood, or even with the blood of a menstruating woman, one should draw the figure of a woman’s misfortune upon birch bark at night using a pen made of a crow’s feather, O beloved, while reciting the name of the target.

On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should draw a beautiful yantra; one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center, surrounded by the letter *ṭha*. There is no limit to the number of *ṭha* letters; one should always surround it with an odd number. Then, having surrounded it with a circle, one should encircle it with the *durbhaga* mantra. By properly installing this yantra in the midst of grass within that house, for as long as that yantra remains in the house, even a hater will become devoted to that resident of the house; of this there is no doubt.

"And this sequence of worship previously described, O Goddess, is always like a blade of grass [to him]. Thus ends the fifth yantra, named "The World-Hater," in the sixth section of the *Śrī-yantracintāmaṇi*.

Śrī Śiva said: "Henceforth I shall describe the yantra for the destruction of enemies. This yantra should be drawn upon a human skull; it should be drawn in a cremation ground on the fourteenth day at the dead of night by one who is alone."
One should draw it on cloth without hesitation; having first drawn it clearly in the middle, one should then smear it with soot both above and below.
It should be drawn using the proper ritual materials and subsequently encircled by a triangle adorned with two lines. O fair-faced one, vertical lines must be made everywhere.
Having placed this yantra inside a pair of earthen saucers (śarāva), one should worship it there with offerings of blood, meat, and flesh, especially with one's own blood. This is the yantra.

Having buried it right there, one should then worship it; one should offer a goat-sacrifice (*ajabali*), and once it has been extracted, one becomes happy. Otherwise, one goes to the city of Yama; there is no doubt about this—no deliberation is required here. Thus ends the first diagram for the destruction of enemies. Śiva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the diagram that destroys life, which effects the death even of a powerful enemy, and not otherwise. [It should be drawn] specifically with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) on a birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*).

A person should write [the mantra] with a crow-feather pen; having written the name of the victim (*sādhya*) within the center of the syllable *hrīṃ*, one should then properly encircle it with a triangle as before. Furthermore, having drawn a trident in each corner, one should then worship it. The procedure for worship is as previously stated in all cases of killing (*māraṇa*). One should bury this well-worshipped yantra inside a hollow bamboo tube in the ground of a cremation ground. Then, by means of that tube and the excellent yantra, his sudden death occurs; of this there is no doubt.

"The previously mentioned seed-mantra of the unfortunate one is also used everywhere for the purpose of killing. Thus ends the second yantra for the killing of enemies in the seventh chapter of the Śrī [Tantra]. Śiva said: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the rite of killing those located in distant lands. One should grind together charcoal from a cremation ground, the blood of a cat, and poison; having ground these, one should write [the mantra] upon a human skull-cup (naraka-pālaka). Having written it as a sealed enclosure, one should write the name of the target in the center, auspiciously enclosed by the syllable *huṃ*, using a pen made from a peacock feather."

Having made that [mandala] eight-petaled, one should likewise draw it in its center; in the four directions, one should write "huṃ phaṭ" in the middle of each petal. Then, one should properly encircle it with two circular lines. Afterwards, O Dear One, one should surround it on all sides with uneven [syllables] starting with "huṃ. Having dug up that [clay] in a auspicious cremation ground and formed it into a hollow vessel as before, one should place it over the fire and worship it according to the instructions. Even for an enemy who has gone to another country, a fever shall arise; it should be burned every day.
"O beautiful one, on whatever day fire is kindled throughout the entire land at night, at that very moment, O beloved, the killing of the enemy occurs.
Thus ends the third yantra, named "The Killing of a Distant Enemy," within the section on killing in the *Cintāmaṇi-yantra*. Śrī Śiva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the killing of all embodied beings. One should specifically draw [the mantra] upon a cloth from a cremation ground, using the blood of a human being and the rubbing of charcoal from a cremation ground. In the cremation ground...

O fair-faced one, having written the name of the target (*sādhya*) enclosed by *huṃ phaṭ* in this manner three times in three lines, one should then properly encircle it with three circular lines. One should fashion an image of the enemy from the dust of the footprint of a crow; having placed the yantra in its center, it should be heated very slowly. By this sequence, the burning and grief of the enemy arise, as well as a great headache on the third day, and a burning sensation in the hands, feet, and limbs, leading to death on the seventh.
"Death occurs; there is no doubt here. The previous procedure is certain—of this there is no uncertainty. Thus ends the fourth yantra, named "The Slayer of All People. Śrī Śiva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra for slaying men and women. One should rub charcoal from a cremation ground onto a leaf of the *vibhītaka* tree and draw [the design] with menstrual blood using a pen made of a crow's feather. One should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) in the center, facing the word "stambha" (paralysis). Then, having drawn a triangle, one should draw a pentagon above it. [Then] a human...

Having cast [the substance] into the center of a *likā* and filled it with clay moistened with that urine, one should worship and fill it as prescribed. Then, a man who carefully buries it in the middle of the earth in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), a fever arises from that; death itself occurs in an instant. One dies within seven nights; otherwise, there is liberation, as previously stated. Thus ends the fifth yantra, titled "The Killing of Men and Women," in the section on killing.

Śrī Śiva said: Now begins the section on eradication (*uccāṭana*). Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme eradication of an enemy. Having written [the mantra] on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*) with the blood of the ring finger, [one should perform the rite of] Gāṇapatya...

One should draw it seedless, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and so forth; having written "huṃ gaṃ" and likewise the name in one row, one should write them in the second row, and then in the third row, a man should write "huṃ gaṃ dhaḥ svāhā" in sequence. Then he should properly enclose that with two lines forming a four-cornered square. O Goddess, the practitioner, wearing red garments and anointed with red sandalwood paste, [should perform this] on the fourteenth day during the Great Rite.

One should perform the worship in sequence with red flowers, red perfumes, and auspicious fruits; there should be a meal for young maidens at night and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability. O beautiful one, a person should daily meditate according to the rite upon the God of gods, Gaṇanātha, who has the luster of blue collyrium, whose trunk is excellent, and who, having seized an enemy by the head, is lifting him up toward the sky in a wondrous manner; he certainly causes [the enemy] to be driven away.

There is no doubt that by this method, using eleven [verses] and twenty [others], this sequence of drawing and worship everywhere effects eradication (*uccāṭana*) once authority has been established. Having divided the diagram (*yantra*) into sections, it is then given mixed with the rice of food-leavings for the crows to eat day after day. Thus ends the first eradication diagram in the section on eradication in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. The venerable Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the eradication of all embodied beings. A person should write [the mantra] on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) with the blood of a crow and an owl; having written the name in the center, he should draw a circle.

Then one should encircle it and subsequently fashion a four-petalled [lotus] adorned with two lines. In the middle of each petal, the letter *ya* is established, ending with the visarga (*visargānta*). The sequence of worship is as previously stated, though devoid of meditation (*dhyāna*). For the purpose of consumption by a crow on the eighth day, the crow indeed departs after abandoning the location; such is the case for the village crow. Thus ends the second yantra, named "The Universal Uccāṭana," in the chapter on Uccāṭana within the Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi. Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme immediate Uccāṭana using poison and *tāla*.

With what [substance] should one draw the crow on a rag from a cremation ground? The previously mentioned procedure for the yantra is prescribed: at night, being self-restrained, one should tie that crow, facing downward and hanging, to a *vibhītaka* tree on the south side. When this is done, on the third day, there shall be an expulsion (*uccāṭana*) from its place. As long as the yantra remains there, the man indeed becomes agitated;
he finds no happiness whatsoever in his house or city, and even his life in a foreign land is in doubt. Thus ends the third yantra, called the "Immediate Expulsion," spoken by Śiva.

And hereafter, I shall describe the supreme rite for the eradication of an enemy. It should be drawn upon a birch-bark leaf with the five juices of the *nimba* tree using a pen made from a crow’s feather; the procedure is exactly as previously stated. Having written the name [of the enemy] in the center, one should then surround it with a circle. One should then fashion a beautiful four-petaled lotus, each petal containing a seed-syllable.
