Having worshipped it as before, one should subsequently bury it face-down according to the previously mentioned ritual. When this is done, on the seventh day, the eradication occurs.

"The ascetic who wanders elsewhere from place to place in this manner is treated with contempt like a blade of grass. Thus ends the fourth yantra, named "The Exorcism of the Enemy," in the section on Exorcism (Uccāṭana). Śiva said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the woman-exorcising yantra. Having written [the name] upon a fruit-stalk with the blood of a donkey and a pen made of a crow's feather, one should surround it with a circle.

Then, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus, beautiful and endowed with seed-syllables. [One should write] the letter *kha* ending with the visarga (*khaḥ*), and after that, the syllable *hrīṃ*. Having thus inscribed the yantra and worshipped it according to the rule..."

Then, having buried it in the ground and filled it up as before, with the [diagram] facing downwards, when this is done, on the third day the enemy's eradication (*uccāṭana*) will occur; for the wind eradicates [him] from his place like a heap of straw. Thus ends the fifth yantra, named "The Eradication of Women," in the section on eradication within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. And Śiva said:

Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme eradication of the three worlds. A man should write [the mantra] on birch bark with the blood of a black cock, and having written the name of the person to be targeted (*sādhya*), he should draw a triangle.

Then, O fair-faced one, one should again draw a second triangle to encircle it. In its upper third part, one should write four *hrīṃ* syllables; likewise, in the [other] three parts, the seed-syllables should be written in numbers equal to those of the sun (twelve). Beyond that, a circle should be drawn, and one should worship it as before. Having prepared the yantra in this manner, one should tie it around the neck of a dog, so that the dog wanders constantly, O fair-faced one. Thus ends the sixth yantra, named "The Uprooting of the Three Worlds," in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śrī Mahādeva said:

Now I shall fully describe this supreme *yantra* for eradication (*uccāṭana*). [It is made] with the juices of the roots and leaves of the night-stalker (*niśācara*)—the night-stalker named Gupta produced from the *haridrā* tree—and with its very thorns. Having fashioned it beautifully with these juices and including the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should then write "phaṭ" in the middle of each petal. After worshipping it according to the rules, one should thereafter worship the *yantra*. It should be given in food and drink; eradication occurs certainly. This is the seventh [chapter], named Eradication.

Śrī Śiva said: [Thus ends the chapter on Uccāṭana in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Now begins the chapter on Protection (*Rakṣā*). Mahādeva said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the yantra named *Ratnākara*, which provides supreme and great protection for children, women, and men. It should be drawn upon a bell-metal plate on an auspicious lunar day and a favorable day, using *rocanā* (yellow pigment), saffron, especially camphor, and well-blended musk; the person should draw it with a stylus made of jasmine wood, starting from the top row.
Having drawn eight horizontal lines and likewise eight vertical ones, forty-nine squares will be correctly formed. The vowels beginning with *a* should be written horizontally and above;
the consonants should be written in sequence, O Dear One, following that same order. Having thus written the seed-syllables (*bījas*), one should then draw tridents.

Above each line, one should certainly write the syllable *kroṃ* in the six [triangles] in the four directions in due order—both in the east and in the west. Having thus worshipped that yantra, one should worship it with the yoga of devotion, O Puṇḍarīka.

With beautiful *śatapatra* lotuses, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *mallikā*, and *ketaka* flowers, as well as *bakula* flowers and auspicious fruits produced in season as they may be available—one should carefully avoid flowers that are odorless or red in color. O Dear One, having thus worshipped for three days with camphor, betel leaves, incense, perfumes, white garments, and various food offerings (*naivedya*), one should daily recite the *Saptaśatī* for three days while feeding Brāhmaṇas with milk-pudding (*pāyasa*) and as much ghee as desired. For three days, one should sleep upon the ground.

O beloved, one should feed one's kinsmen; having extracted [the substance], made it into a pill, and then encased it with the three metals (triloha), one should prepare that pill with the remaining liquid and water, O fair-faced goddess. One should wear this yantra on the root of the arm or at the throat. By wearing that yantra, afflictions (upasarga) are pacified, as well as misfortune (alakṣmī), quarrels, and especially ill-fortune. Whatever has been done by another, all of that perishes. This is known as the Śāntika and Pauṣṭika rite, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. First, the yantra...

"Known as the 'King of the Three Worlds,' it produces immediate conviction. Thus ends the first yantra, named "The Protector of Children," in the section on Peaceful Rites within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. The venerable Mahādeva said: "Listen, O Brahmin, I shall describe the yantra that wards off thieves. When this yantra is placed upon the palm of the hand, there is no fear of snakes or tigers. The method of drawing is according to the previous rule, and the materials are exactly as previously stated.

Indeed, for the attainment of peace everywhere, no other [method] exists that is superior. The worship is as previously described, and the observances (*niyama*) are likewise; [it should be drawn] upon birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*)."

This second diagram is a supreme yantra. In its center, within the heart of the syllable *hrīṃ*, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) is established. At its base, one should properly join the letter *a*, followed by the letters *la*, *va*, and ending with *ya*. This is conjoined with the vowel *ī* and is the beautiful seed-syllable of peace (*śānti-bīja*). Then, one should correctly encircle it with two lines forming a four-cornered square. Having encased it in the three metals, one should wear it at the root of the arm; it destroys the fear of snakes and tigers.

"It destroys fear of thieves as well as various calamities; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. Thus ends the second yantra in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*, titled "The Warding Off of Snakes, Tigers, and Thieves. Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra that destroys misfortune, especially for women and always for men. As for its drawing, it is exactly as previously stated; the pen is as previously specified, and the birch-bark [is the surface].

A person should draw three lines and write the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Above that, one should draw a triangle with two lines, and above that, a quadrangle adorned with two lines.

Then, according to the previously mentioned method, one should place tridents in each corner. Having encased it in the three metals (*triloha*), a woman or a man should wear it according to the prescribed rite on the root of the arm or on the neck. It destroys various calamities, enables a barren woman to conceive, and having attained incomparable good fortune, one becomes like a god.
Thus ends the third yantra, named *Saubhāgyavardhana*, in the section on Peace (*śāntyadhikāra*) of the *Datesadā*. Śrī Mahādeva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme yantra that utterly destroys fever—specifically that great fever born of spirits (*bhūta*) and living beings which is described in the medical treatises (*vaidyaka*). This yantra for the destruction of fever must always be prepared with effort. It should be drawn upon a cloth from a cremation ground using the juices of a madman. On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having worshipped it, one should then bury it.

A man, remaining without food, should go to a cremation ground during the day. There, he should draw a four-cornered figure with four divisions above it, such that it becomes eight-petaled. Having written the name in the center, enclosed within the syllable *rakāra*, he should write [the mantra] upon the petals, each adorned with the syllable *rakāra* and a bindu.

Having worshipped all the lines there in their proper sequence and having covered the ground with pleasing offerings of flowers and oblations, the most terrible fever caused by those spirits departs at that very moment.

Thus ends the fourth yantra, named "The Destroyer of Fever," in the Chapter on Peace within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śiva said: Hereafter, I shall describe the most excellent yantra which brings peace to children, provides protection, and destroys all calamities. It should be drawn according to the previously stated procedure using the aforementioned materials in due order; one should write it upon birch bark and perform worship according to the previously stated rite, having first inscribed the syllable *Nāma* (the Name) in the center.

Then one should encircle a circle, and thereafter an eight-petalled lotus should be fashioned, beautiful and endowed with seed-syllables (*bīja*). One should place the letters beginning with *sa* and ending with the visarga (*ḥ*) upon each petal individually. After worshipping it according to the prescribed rites, one should then wear this king of yantras—encased in the three metals (*triloha*)—either on the root of the arm or on the forehead. By wearing this king of yantras, Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and others likewise abandon the child and depart. Thus ends the fifth yantra, which provides protection for children, in the chapter on pacification (*śānti*) within the *Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śrī Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the third...

The destroyer of the performer of sacrifices (the *yajvāra*) should be drawn with the previously mentioned substances upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf. Having written the letter *ya* in the center, one should surround it within a triangle; then, one should write the seed-syllables (*bījas*).

Below that, a svastika should be made, and all of that should again be surrounded by a four-cornered figure shaped like a crest (*śikhā*). Thereupon, the wise one should inscribe the letter *ya*, ending with the visarga, arranged unevenly therein.

At that time, having performed worship, one should tie [this amulet] on the right hand for the sake of pacifying *velājvara* and for the sake of strength; by means of curd-rice (*dadhibhakta*), whether a child or an elder, one shall be freed from fever at that very moment. There is no doubt that the fever born of spirits (*bhūtaja*) or the tertian (*tṛtīyaka*) fever departs; however, that which is born of disease (*rogaja*) does not depart, and therefore it should not be applied there by the wise. Thus ends the sixth yantra, the destroyer of tertian fever, in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śrī.

Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the destroyer of fever at the [specific] time. It should be drawn with the substances and in the sequence previously mentioned, according to the aforementioned ritual. Having drawn it upon birch bark and worshipped it according to the rules, one should write the letter *Nā* (Na) in the center and surround it with a circle. Above, below, and likewise on the back, there should be a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure) of the letter *Ka*. Then, an eight-petaled lotus should be made, endowed everywhere with seed-syllables (*bīja*). In the middle of each petal, the letter *Na* adorned with a nasal dot (*bindu*) should be placed. Between the petals, one should place eight instances of the syllable *Hrīṃ* everywhere. Having thus drawn and worshipped it, [one should proceed with] the cooling...

Then one should apply it; within three days the patient suffering from fever and burning sensations will undoubtedly be liberated. When applied in warm water, the cold fever is destroyed. If it is bound to the base of the hand, the fever arising at its specific time is destroyed; of this there is no doubt, O beautiful goddess, [it happens] at that very moment. Thus ends the seventh yantra, titled "The Destroyer of Time-bound Fever," in the Chapter on Peace (*śāntyadhikāra*) of the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the protection for children at all times, a yantra for the purpose of protecting against fire and wind.

The practitioner should write the name of the person to be accomplished (the sādhya) within a circle using the previously mentioned procedure. Then, he should properly enclose it with two lines forming a square. Above that, he should draw a square and inscribe tridents at each corner. At the end of each corner, the wise one should write the seed-syllable *ṭha*, adorned with a nasal dot (*bindu*). Between the upper and lower [lines], he should inscribe the syllable *hrīṃ*. Having thus written this yantra and worshipped it according to the rules, and having encased it in three metals, he should wear it around his neck. By doing so, no afflictions whatsoever—whether physical, mental, or caused by envy—shall arise.
"How can there be anger or disease, and how could teeth emerge [in such a state]? The defect of breast milk never afflicts the child.

Thus ends the eighth yantra, named "Protection of the Child from Fire," in the section on propitiatory rites (*śāntyadhikāra*) within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śrī Śiva said: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the destroyer of spirits (*bhūta*) and epilepsy (*apasmāra*). If one is seized by *śākinīs*, *bhūtas*, or terrible *vetālas*, then for the sake of liberation from them, one should fashion a captivating yantra. If one who is healthy should perform it, he will not be seized by those defects. By means of the materials previously mentioned..."

O fair-faced one, having again written [the mantra] in the middle on a birch-bark leaf according to the previously stated procedure, one should properly encircle it with a circle and then write eight petals upon it. Furthermore, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center of each petal. Having thus inscribed that yantra, it should be encased in three metals—gold, silver, and copper—which are known as the "three metals" (*triloha*). This Tripurabhairava yantra should be worn around the necks of children; O auspicious lady, by doing so, the child is liberated from diseases such as epilepsy (*apasmāra*) and other ailments. Thus ends the section on pacification (*śāntyadhikāra*) in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*.

The Ninth Yantra, named "Removal of Forgetfulness. Śrī Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme protection against serpents. O Goddess, when a child or even an adult is not seen by the lord of serpents due to the negligence of those snakes, one should draw [the yantra] according to the previously mentioned method and worship it according to the rules. Having written the syllable *Nāma* in the center and surrounded it with two circular lines, one should enclose eight petals provided with the seed-syllable *Haṃsa*. Having encased it in three metals, one should wear it at the root of the arm; then [the dangers] perish upon sight.

If, through negligence, one’s foot should fall upon venomous serpents in the four directions, one should restrain them; of this there is no doubt. Even if bitten through negligence, the poison will not take hold.

This is the *yantra* spoken by Garuḍa for the purpose of restraining snakes. Thus ends the tenth *yantra*, named "The Restraining of Snakes," in the section on Peace (*śāntyadhikāra*) within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*.

Śiva said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme method for terrifying the *ḍākinīs*. When a man or even a woman is seized by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like, or by *śākinīs* and *brahmarākṣasas*—or by anyone else—[this method shall be applied].

Furthermore, one should then construct this machine for the purpose of terrifying the *bhūtas* and *rākṣasas*. Having drawn it well with chalk on a cloth or upon the ground—drawing four horizontal lines and five vertical ones—there will thus be twelve squares, O fair-faced lady. Having written the syllable *drīṃ* in each square, one should then worship it with offerings of oblations and flowers, and light a lamp there (upon it). Having established it over a fire, one should kindle it with wood; then the great *bhūta*, weeping and trembling, departs.

At that very moment, having released the child and abandoned the region, he departs. Thus ends the eleventh yantra, named "Terrifying Spirits," in the section on pacification within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*.

The Lord said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme method for the total destruction of fever. It should be inscribed upon a betel leaf with the thorns of a *kauṇapa* (cane-thorn). Having written the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*), it should be auspiciously enclosed by the syllable *kroṃ*. One should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) in each of the centers of a hexagon, and above each corner, one should draw the *hrīṃ* syllable all around.

Having worshipped it according to the sequence of the field (*khetkrama*) and for the purpose of chewing betel, it is offered; O Goddess, by the consumption of this yantra, fever departs—of this there is no doubt. It must be consumed exclusively; no hesitation should be made here. Thus ends the twelfth yantra, the destroyer of intermittent fever, in the chapter on pacification (*śāntyadhikāra*) of the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*.

The venerable Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme protector of the fetus. O fair-faced one, it should be drawn with elephant-ichor upon a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*). Of the elephant...
One should draw [the diagram] with saffron mixed with *tumada* (a type of resin). Having drawn a circle in the center with *nāma* (the name), one should enclose it with four corners using two lines.

A circular pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be made in the four directions. The syllable *ya* and the syllable *ra*, each ending in the visarga (*visargānta*), should be written separately in the middle of the pericarp as before; then one should worship it. Enclosing it with iron, one should place it around the neck of a pregnant woman. There will be a comfortable delivery, and the pain of labor will perish. Thus ends the section on peace in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*.

The Thirteenth Yantra: For Protection from the Fears of Censure and Embryonic Development. Śrī Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the protection for a pregnant woman, a yantra that wards off pain in the womb and ensures a safe delivery. It should be drawn according to the previously mentioned procedure, using the aforementioned substances and materials in due order, upon a birch bark (bhūrjapatra) by a skilled person following the prescribed rite. In the center, one should write the Praṇava (Oṃ) and the syllable Drīṃ, enclosing the name [of the woman] at the beginning and the end. Like a cloth, it should be surrounded by four long lines forming a square, and above...

One should draw three triangles, each established in one corner. One should write *drīṃ*, *kṣūṃ*, and *drīṃ* located within the corners; likewise, one should write *kroṃ* and *śrīṃ* in the remaining petals.

Having thus drawn and worshipped it, encased in the three metals, this yantra should undoubtedly be worn around the neck of a pregnant woman. Yoni-pain, headache, and afflictions caused by spirits (*bhūta-doṣa*) are destroyed; there is no doubt that an easy delivery occurs, free from suffering. This is declared the King of Yantras, a secret [teaching] originating from Śiva.
Thus ends the fourteenth yantra in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*, within the section on pacification (*śāntyadhikāra*), which brings about the easy delivery of pregnant women. Śiva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme *Sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala, which provides all protection and removes deceit and defects. A wise man should draw five vertical lines and five horizontal lines; he should understand that there are sixteen squares in total. Having written the vowels beginning with 'A' in sequence in every square, [one should write] at night on a leaf of birch-bark with musk... [the syllables] *bhūta-ja-hni*. *(Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available text.)*

One should mix yellow orpiment with snow (ice) and draw [the yantra] in sequence; having worshipped it with various flowers, fragrances, pleasing incenses, and diverse offerings, one should worship the Brahmins with garments and wealth.

Then, filled with devotion, that person—whose mind is joyful and who acts according to the rules—should enclose the yantra with the three metals and wear it at the root of the right arm, or a woman should diligently wear this excellent yantra around her neck. By wearing it, having obtained the grace of the Lord, he becomes beloved by all, endowed with fortune, perfectly fulfilled, and free from all fear in the world.

Thus, having attained the eight great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*), the sixteenth yantra, named "The All-Protecting Increaser of Good Fortune," in the chapter on Peace (*śāntyadhikāra*) within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*, has reached its conclusion. The venerable Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra that brings victory in gambling. By wearing this yantra, victory in all forms of gambling is declared. It should be drawn upon a palm leaf (*tāla*) with a horse's hoof-print; it consists of sixty-four squares. O Goddess, by wearing it, victory is certainly attained everywhere. It should be inscribed on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) with a stylus (*lekhanī*).

O lady of pure smiles, having made ink from the soot of a lamp-wick using a cotton wick (*kapiñchaya*), one should draw at night nine lines—horizontal and vertical—that are well-spaced. Thus, O fair-faced one, sixty-four squares are formed. In the center, the seed-syllables (*bīja*) should be written in both direct and reverse order. Furthermore, those very same syllables should be written again according to the sequence of mind and intellect. This wonderful arrangement of words was composed by Dāmodara, the lord of poets. *Makhe raktaṃ dayatuṣṭā kajinaṃ taṃ danīvinaḥ*—this is the meter; this is the mantra for the victory of those who desire liberation through the path of speech. These very thirty-two seed-syllables are to be inscribed.

By the lord of poets Dāmodara, the *Vājikrama* has been composed in three ways according to his own will; by means of which the sixty-four squares are traversed by people at their pleasure. Incidentally, this charming *Yaṃtrarāja*, which brings victory in all gambling, has been described by me; through its retention, victory is certainly attained. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, named "Victory in Gambling," in the section on Peace (*Śāntyadhikāra*) within the *Śrī Yaṃtracintāmaṇi*. The venerable Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the captivating *Bandhamokṣa* (the release from bondage).

By whose grace one who is bound and obstructed is thus liberated in an instant—when someone is blocked by anyone else and finds no liberation for themselves, then they should fashion this *yantra*, which bestows liberation at that very moment. O lady of pure smiles, this supreme *yantra* should be carefully inscribed with camphor and saffron on a birch leaf in a secluded place. Having first written the *nāma* (name) in the center, and immediately after that the *hṛllekhā* mantra, one should then properly encircle it in a circle.

One should cause [the disciple] to release [the breath] with two lines and encircle it on all four sides; having encircled the four corners with three lines, it should be worshipped with effort using perfumes, flowers, and auspicious fruits. Having encased it in the three metals (triloha), one should wear it at the base of the arm or on the neck.

By wearing it, one is instantly liberated from saṃsāra and becomes free from the sense of "mine" (nirmama). Through constant wearing, there is never any obstruction to one's well-being; of this there is no doubt, even in dreams.

Thus, in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*, within the section on Peace (*śāntyadhikāra*), ends the eighteenth yantra, named "Liberation from Bondage" (*bandhamokṣaṇa*). The venerable Mahādeva said: "Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the destruction of bondage through the *Bava* [yantra], which indeed leads to the state of Nirvāṇa and bestows the state of detachment (*nirveda*). One should establish the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) in the center of a hexagon, having enclosed it with the *niḥsāra* [mantra].

Having written the *niḥsāra* upon a wide birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*), one should write it within the corners with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron, and sandalwood. Then, with true devotion and self-restraint, one should worship the yantra according to the prescribed rules."

A man, having placed [this yantra] in the midst of iron, should always wear it upon his head; by wearing it, he gradually becomes detached from worldly things and, having attained the yoga of knowledge, is liberated—of this there is no doubt.

He becomes free from delusion regarding son, friend, and wife. Whether in a desolate house, a forest, a difficult pass, a town, or a mountain, he is born [as such]; of this there is no doubt—the yogi is honored everywhere. Thus ends the nineteenth yantra, named "Liberation from Saṃsāra," in the chapter on Peace within the *Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śiva said: Now...

I shall now fully explain the liberation from wicked beings. When one is afflicted by wicked beings in a forest, a river, or a difficult terrain, one should then fashion this *yantra* upon the palm of the left hand. Having performed the worship of the syllable *drīṃ* mentally with saliva, one should sprinkle blood born of passion (*anāmodbhava*) in the four directions. At that very moment, the creature is liberated—even if obstructed by leopards, great serpents, wolves, elephants, or other wicked beings; of this there is no doubt. [Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Liberation from Wicked Beings," in the section on Peace within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*.]

This *Tama-yantra* is completed, and this section on Peace (*śānty-adhikāra*) is finished. Now begins the section on Bondage and Liberation (*bandha-mokṣa-adhikāra*). People bound from head to foot, their limbs tightly encircled by fetters, attain liberation in an instant by his command—the one before whom gods, humans, and *siddhas* in the world bow with minds humbled by devotion. With a mind bowed in devotion, I prostrate to him, the prisoner. I shall declare this great section which effects the release of prisoners among men; through faith in it, O Goddess, all undertakings are accomplished instantly. Śrī Mahādeva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain...

This is the accomplishment of liberation from bondage; by its grace, liberation from bondage arises in an instant. Having written the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*), one should write four *drīṃ* syllables. Then, one should properly encircle that with a single circular line. This yantra should be drawn upon a cake and smeared with ghee. There, one should worship it with various flowers and food offerings (*naivedya*). For the purpose of consumption, the cake should be given to the deity.

"O beautiful one, a living being is released in three days; even one firmly bound is released. Thus ends the first yantra, "The Release of the Bound," in the section on liberation within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. Śiva said: *Aiṃ drīṃ drīṃ drīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ vaṃdī devyai amukasya bandha-mokṣaṃ kuru kuru mātar namaḥ svāhā.* Having uttered this mantra while grasping the name [of the person], one should offer oblations of guggulu into the fire for Caṇḍikā with each repetition of the mantra for twenty-seven days. Having offered the oblation repeatedly every day with the mantra until the end of twenty-seven days, liberation occurs; it is not otherwise. Only this single yantra is prescribed.

"If one should offer oblations with clarified butter," thus [ends] the second yantra, named "The Liberator from Bondage and the Like," in the section on Liberation within the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. The venerable Mahādeva said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra for the release from shackles (*nigaḍamocana*), by the grace of which one bound by the hands, feet, or neck is liberated. It should be drawn upon a bell-metal plate (*kāṃsyapātra*) using yellow pigment (*rocanā*), sandalwood paste, camphor, saffron, and musk. One should place the syllable *drīṃ* in the center and surround it with a circle; then, one should surround that with a sixteen-petaled lotus provided with the vowels beginning with 'a'. Then, one should properly surround that...

Furthermore, upon that [circle], one should draw a circular line provided with thirty-two petals. One should write the consonants in order, beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*. Having established the great worship with perfumes, flowers, auspicious fruits, food offerings (*naivedya*), oblations (*bali*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and charming gifts of lamps, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra: *oṃ namaścaṇḍikāyai svāhā*. This should be performed daily with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), honey, sugar, and especially with *guggulu* resin; it is completed on the seventh day. Then, having drawn out all the milk from the vessel, [one should apply] perfume and [other] pleasing substances.

Half a pill should be given for the purpose of drinking, and one should not prepare it otherwise; by wearing it, even a man who has been bound for a long time shall be liberated. Thus ends the second yantra, named "Liberation from Shackles," in the section on Liberation from Bonds in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*. The venerable Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra that releases bonds;

by its grace, even one who is confined in a prison is liberated. One should write the syllable *drīṃ* in the center of the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*), having written it upon birch bark with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*).

Having worshipped that yantra, one should cast it into flowing water; with that water, one should provide him a meal of cooked food. When this is done, on the third day he is liberated—of this there is no doubt.

Even one who is in a hole, one who is confined, or one who is hidden, is set free. [Thus ends the third yantra, named "The Liberation of the Hidden," in the seventh section of the Mokṣādhikāra in the *Śrī Yantracintāmaṇi*.

And thus the Mokṣādhikāra is complete. The ritual manual (*kalpa*) named *Yantracintāmaṇi*, spoken by the venerable Śiva, bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, and kāma, and destroys the faction of enemies.

The person who constantly worships this or wears it shall become invincible to all the worlds; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, the righteous man who always listens to this while it is being recited shall likewise become worthy of worship and honor; of this there is no doubt. It is certain that whoever hears of this *Cintāmaṇi* Yantra but develops no faith in it will surely become a sinner, a hater, and ill-fated in this world. But for one who, endowed with faith, takes refuge in this *Cintāmaṇi* Yantra—who, desiring to live, would ever create enmity with him? What more need be said beyond this?

By the power of the mantra proclaimed by Śiva, he who possesses a beautiful form governs the world, shining most brilliantly with that splendor. This merit-bestowing, purifying, supreme secret, which is the very essence of all, has been proclaimed by me. It is the *Cintāmaṇi*, the accomplisher of desired tasks, the means for achieving visible results and other fruits. They declare the first chapter to be on Subjugation (*vaśya*), the second on Attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), the third on Paralysis (*staṃbhana*), the fourth on Enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), the fifth on Killing (*māraṇa*), the sixth on Expulsion (*uccāṭana*), the seventh on Peace (*śāntika*), and the eighth on the Favor of Captives (*vandīprasāda*). Thus they speak of these eight chapters in this ritual manual (*kalpa*).
That jewel, well-worshipped by the best of gods—[Thus ends the Yantracintāmaṇi composed by the King of Pandits, Śrī Dāmodara, the executor of Śiva’s command]. May there be auspiciousness!
